etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English restoren, from Old French restorer, from Latin rēstaurāre, equivalent to re- +‎ store.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To reestablish, or bring back into existence.
(transitive) To bring back to good condition from a state of decay or ruin.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Mark iii:5:
quote.text: and his hand was restored whole as the other

quote.citation: 1718, Mat[thew] Prior, “Solomon on the Vanity of the World. A Poem in Three Books.”, in Poems on Several Occasions, London:  […]  Jacob Tonson […], and John Barber […], →OCLC, (please specify the page):
quote.text: our fortune restored after the severest afflictions

definitions.definition: (transitive) To give or bring back (that which has been lost or taken); to bring back to the owner; to replace.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Genesis xx:7:
quote.text: Now therefore restore the man his wife.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book I”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: Loss of Eden, till one greater man / Restore us, and regain the blissful seat.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “Tityrus and Meliboeus”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The father banish;d virtue shall restore.

quote.citation: 1769, Firishta, translated by Alexander Dow, Tales translated from the Persian of Inatulla of Delhi, volume I, Dublin: P. and W. Wilson et al., page iv:
quote.text: The plain appears like paradiſe reſtored, where the proud cypreſs and tall arreca ſeem walking by the margin of the paſſing ſtream.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To give in place of, or as restitution for.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Exodus xxii:1:
quote.text: He shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep.

definitions.definition: (transitive, computing) To recover (data, etc.) from a backup.
(transitive, music) To bring (a note) back to its original signification.
(obsolete) To make good; to make amends for.

quote.citation: 1609, William Shakespeare, “Sonnet 30”, in Shake-speares Sonnets. […], London: By G[eorge] Eld for T[homas] T[horpe] and are to be sold by William Aspley, →OCLC:
quote.text: But if the while I think on thee, dear friend, / All losses are restored, and sorrows end.

definitions.definition: (computing) The act of recovering data or a system from a backup.
